newsitem.title: USA: Hanwa reinforces Japan low-rate expectations in US.
newsitem.headline: Hanwa reinforces Japan low-rate expectations in US.

text.p: Japanese government plans to suspend a bank's operations for the first time since World War II prompted U.S. experts to speculate that Japan's financial system remains too weak for higher interest rates.
"It reminds us that there is still some sensitivity to interest rate changes," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc in New York.
"And if these problems are perhaps more widespread than the failure of one bank suggests, then Bank of Japan may not be rushed into raising interest rates," Iggo added.

Earlier, Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) confirmed on Wednesday that it will order Hanwa Bank, a second-tier regional bank operating mainly in the Osaka region, to suspend all business except for deposit withdrawals. Failure to recover bad loans prompted the action, the MOF said.
The news reminds financial markets that "Japan is not out of the woods yet," Iggo said.
Japan's financial sector is riddled with non-performing loans, many from the real estate sector.

The Bank of Japan has kept official rates at rockbottom levels so Japanese banks can borrow cheaply and lend out at higher levels. U.S. experts said Wednesday's news reinforces the view that the policy will not change any time soon.

After the MOF issues its order on Thursday, the Bank of Japan will establish an emergency fund to help the failed bank cope with the rush of withdrawals on its deposits, a source close to the Japanese government told Reuters.
While Hanwa is the first bank to come under a government suspension order since World War II, some other financial institutions have already met a similar fate.
High Frequency Economics chief economist Carl Weinberg pointed out that a bank failure differs from a corporate failure in that the liabilities are not likely to be secured by equities.
"Therefore, it's unlikely that there will be a liquidation of stocks that were put up as collateral against loans at this institution," he added.
Weinberg said he is not as alarmed about the possible risk to the stock market as he was a few weeks ago when a finance company went belly-up.
"I think it's still bad, but it's not as terrifying as it could be," Weinberg said.
The foreign exchange market's knee-jerk reaction was to sell yen and buy dollars, according to dealers.
The dollar soared to a session high of 111.68 yen before closing at 111.48/58, up from 111.15/20.
"It's the kind of thing that just makes people nervous about Japan and the financial system and makes them think they want to take their money elsewhere," Weinberg said.
